particulars: All names, dates, places, ages, sentence lengths, stab-wound counts, the 21-day deadline and the governors' names are absent; the reading is set in a different domain entirely (a platform or agency notice about a fringe group).

items.record: The case is a wrongful criminal conviction for rape and murder: "Rebecca Lynn Williams... was raped and stabbed over thirty times" and Washington was sentenced to death.
items.reading: A platform company or regulator issues a policy enforcement notice about a diffuse fringe movement.
items.loss: The basic nature of the event and of the institution (criminal justice, a capital prosecution) is misidentified.

items.record: The opposing party is one intellectually disabled man who "would politely defer to any authority figure," not a group.
items.reading: A diffuse, loosely organized fringe of scattered individuals sharing a grievance.
items.loss: The target is a single vulnerable person, and his particular vulnerability is what drives the outcome; the reading misdescribes this.

items.record: Police extracted a confession over two days of questioning, and only "on the fourth attempt at a rehearsed confession did authorities accept Washington's statement."
items.loss: The mechanism by which the authorities built the account, through coaching and repeated takes, is missing.

items.record: The confession contradicted known facts: he did not know "the race of his victim, the address... or that he had raped her."
items.reading: The statement is described as cooperative, clear and "not obviously deceptive."
items.loss: The record shows an authoritative narrative that was internally false and visibly contradicted by the evidence.

items.record: Police took him to the scene three times and "in the end had to help him pick out Williams' apartment."
items.loss: The sequence of authorities physically steering the suspect to produce corroboration is lost.

items.record: Four other confessions were dismissed "because of the inconsistencies," yet the fifth was kept.
items.loss: The selective acceptance of the same unreliable method when it suited one case is missing.

items.record: Evidence was altered: after he became a suspect, "an amended forensic report was prepared (without additional testing being conducted)" calling the result "inconclusive."
items.reading: The "rationalizing" stance is read as justifying enforcement already decided.
items.loss: The concrete mechanism of rationalization, rewriting exculpatory evidence to fit a chosen suspect, is not recovered.

items.record: The adversarial process failed: "only the State's psychologist testified," and at the penalty phase "the defense did not offer any counter argument."
items.loss: The collapse of the defense side, which left the institution unopposed, is missing.

items.record: Rescue came through an informal network of outsiders: another death row inmate alerted "Marie Deans (a non-lawyer...)" and a visiting lawyer, whose firm won a stay "nine days before he was scheduled to die."
items.reading: Eventual resolution through attrition, migration of the fringe, or external pressure.
items.loss: The specific route of rescue, through peers and volunteers outside the system reaching inside it at the last moment, is missing.

items.record: DNA excluded him in 1993, but he "was time barred by Virginia law" and received only a commutation to life.
items.loss: The procedural rule that kept the institution from correcting itself despite proof of innocence is not recovered.

items.record: Correction came slowly, in steps from successive governors: commutation, then a pardon "on limited grounds," then years later "an absolute pardon" acknowledging he was wrongfully convicted.
items.reading: The institution issues further clarifications, each more rationalizing than the last; the matter likely never resolves.
items.loss: The record shows partial, reluctant retreat by executive discretion ending in a full admission, which is the opposite of the escalation the reading predicts.

items.record: The real offender was later identified: "Kenneth Tinsley... pleaded guilty to Rebecca Lynn Williams' rape and murder."
items.loss: The final resolution of the underlying question of truth is missing.

items.record: The person wronged reacted mildly: "This was a whole lot better than I expected."
items.reading: The target experiences the action as cold, faceless, and proof of persecution, and becomes more mobilized.
items.loss: The emotional response of the person harmed is misdescribed: he shows modest gratitude, not grievance or radicalization.

items.record: The stakes were life and death: a death sentence with "a September execution date imminent."
items.reading: Stakes are listed as unknown, with restriction of accounts as the likely penalty.
items.loss: The scale of the harm at stake, execution of an innocent person, is not recovered.
